### Season outlook as written in the guide (p. 144)

It’s going to be strange seeing Utah without Kyle Whittingham. The two-time Pac-12 Coach of the Year has been with the Utes since 1994, and he did a good job of maintaining the standard of excellence that Urban Meyer put in place in his two years with the program (2003 and 2004). It is, however, Whittingham’s right-hand man that is taking over in Utah, as longtime defensive coordinator Morgan Scalley, who has been with the program since 2007, will get his crack at the top job. Scalley has been tremendous coaching up the Utes’ defense, and there’s no reason he can’t continue the tradition of winning in Salt Lake City. This year’s team is actually plenty talented, but the fact that Whittingham went to Michigan did make things interesting. Whittingham took offensive coordinator Jason Beck with him to Ann Arbor, and some players followed — including defensive stars John Henry Daley and Smith Snowden. Under 8.5 It’s always incredibly difficult for road teams to win games at Rice-Eccles Stadium, and Utah definitely has some impressive top-end talent on both sides of the ball. However, the Utes lost a legendary coach in Whittingham, they seem weaker in the trenches than usual, and Dampier’s arm abandoned him in big games last year. All of that makes it a little hard to buy into this team winning nine games. This team seems a little more likely to trip up in coin-flip games, or even lose some games you’d normally expect the Utes to win. The Arkansas game on September 12 should teach us quite a bit about the group.

## 26. Open Questions / Risks

The guide's *Three Burning Questions for the 2026 Season* *(p. 145)*, with the answers as written:

### What’s going on at the quarterback position?

Devon Dampier is back for the Utes after throwing for 2,490 yards with 24 touchdowns and only five interceptions last year. He also rushed for 835 yards and 10 scores. Dampier is a dynamic dual-threat option under center, and he showed some minor improvements in accuracy during his first season with Utah. However, this team is going to give Byrd Ficklin snaps to see what he can do. At times, this approach will be tough for opponents to stop, but what happens when Utah faces elite defenses? As the saying goes, “when you have two quarterbacks, you really have none.” Will the Utes be able to consistently convert in key third-and- long situations? If not, their schedule could get the better of them.

### Will the offensive line be this team’s Achilles heel?

Utah normally has big, burly dudes along the offensive line, and blocking is rarely an issue with this program. However, the Utes don’t return a single starter from last year’s team, and the only projected starter who was consistently starting games in 2025 is Montana State transfer Cedric Jefferson. Utah does have some impressive young pieces to play up front this year, including true freshman Kelvin Obot. He looks the part of a future pro. But there’s nothing that suggests this will be one of the better units in the Big 12, and this offense won’t look great without strong blocking.

### Is this defense good enough for the Utes to compete at the highest level?

It’s brutal that Scalley was this team’s defensive coordinator last year, yet the team wasn’t able to keep Snowden and Henry Daley around. The Utes now enter the season with some major concerns on defense, which is quite new for a program that is consistently excellent on this side of the ball. Utah only has four returning starters in the projected lineup, and it’s the defensive line and linebackers that look shaky. The Utes should be extremely tough to throw against, but will they be able to stop the run? That’s looking like a potential weakness, and being unable to stop opponents from picking up chunk yardage has a trickle-down effect that impacts the secondary.
